title: AI in the Judiciary: Power, Limits, and the Social Contract — Judge Scott Schlegel on the Texas Appellate Law Podcast (E164)
pub: Texas Appellate Law Podcast E164 (hosts Todd Smith & Jody Sanders; produced by LawPods)
author: Scott Schlegel

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Schlegel accepts the cluster’s human-led, selective-deployment proposition and materially extends it to courts: technology should improve administration rather than replace judicial judgment, with safeguards calibrated to user experience and institutional risk. He adds a distinctive social-contract and consent-based boundary for AI adjudication.
qs: So, some of the, I wrote this morning, I don't know if y'all saw it, build a frictionless system and then find out where friction needs to be placed back in.

kp.k: Court modernisation should reduce barriers, not replace judgment
kp.d: Schlegel frames technology as a means to make justice more efficient, effective and accessible rather than replace judges. As historical examples, he reports introducing an online calendar in 2014, scheduling and reminders costing $150 annually, and a Squarespace information website costing $300. He says staggered criminal appearance times and reminders improved participation, but supplies no measured reduction in failures to appear and explicitly says he did not survey users. These are operational experiences, not evidence of AI's effects.
qs: We're not talking about human judgment. We're not talking about replacing judges.
Technology to advance justice is what I propose and what I'm a proponent of.
I can't hear 100 cases at 9 a.m. So why am I making 100 people come to my courtroom and cause mayhem?
And then I would send them text and email reminders to cut down on failures to appear.

kp.k: Judicial AI deployment faces infrastructure and budget constraints
kp.d: Schlegel describes his appellate court's existing digitised case-management system as a foundation for future AI use. Almost three years into his appellate tenure, the court is exploring on-premises AI servers to support central staff on civil cases and clerk's-office intake. This remains a budget-dependent proposal, not a completed deployment; individual court budgets and competing building-maintenance needs constrain implementation.
qs: Everything was digitized.
And now, almost three years in, we're looking at an on-prem AI servers where we can code it and train it and help out with central staff on civil cases.
Now I'm looking for the budget to do it and going forward.
Each court has their own budget.

kp.k: Trusted software integration may accelerate judicial AI adoption
kp.d: Schlegel predicts broader chambers adoption as AI becomes embedded in software courts already trust, including legal-research systems and enterprise office tools. He attributes earlier obstacles to token costs, unaffordable implementations and discomfort with unfamiliar products. He also describes more experienced users seeking less restrictive tools, while recommending progression according to competence rather than immediate access to maximum capability.
qs: The tokens cost way too much and there was just not a comfortable level of using tools that we aren't familiar with.
And so I've always said until the tools get baked into the tools that the courts trust, you won't see adoption for the chambers.
You're going to start seeing adoption going forward.
I always joke that you should have to level up before you touch the next tool.

kp.k: Judges should understand cases before consulting generative AI
kp.d: Schlegel's judicial guidelines prescribe independent engagement with the file before AI-assisted drafting. His law-clerk and first-year-associate analogy treats AI as assistance whose work cannot replace the judge's own examination. He prefers enterprise products, discourages free tools and describes his guidelines as precautions rather than technical instructions.
qs: Rule one of AI, don't use AI. Do your job first. Get a direction, get a feel, understand the file.
Don't just put it into a GenAI bot and say, what's the answer?
You'd never rely upon a first year associate for anything.
And you're going to walk through it.

kp.k: Judicial AI Consortium supports confidential peer learning
kp.d: Schlegel describes a judges-only initiative conceived by Judge Maritza Braswell with his and Judge Xavier Rodriguez's involvement. At the interview date, he reports over 200 judges signed up, over 100 attending the initial meeting and about 20 attending the first shorter pop-in. Meetings are unrecorded, and participation is US-only for now. Its intended remit includes tools, settings, policies, drafting, administration and access to justice; these are learning objectives, not demonstrated outcomes.
qs: Judges only ask stupid questions. Talk to each other about how you're using it.
Again, we're not recording anything. It's just a conversation for judges.
We had over 100 uh judges from across the country.
we've already got over 200 people, over 200 judges who have signed up.
We've had international judges who have wanted to sign up and we're keeping it to the US only for now.

kp.k: Internal disclosure addresses unusually consequential judicial hallucinations
kp.d: Schlegel describes his court's policy as permitting specified uses with approved products while requiring staff to tell their judge. He argues judicial errors carry distinctive institutional risks because they can become law or precedent. He knows of three judicial hallucination incidents, including two recalled federal opinions and a lawyer-prepared state order, but acknowledges incomplete knowledge and uncertainty about the state case's appellate treatment. This is anecdotal reporting, not a prevalence estimate.
qs: You may use AI in these situations with these approved products, and you must tell your judge that you used it.
When we mess up, it's the law. It could become precedent.
I only know of three, not that it hasn't done more.
You've got the two federal judge opinions that had to be recalled.
That order contained hallucinated cases. The judge signed it without checking it.

kp.k: Existing professional duties generally suffice for attorney AI use
kp.d: Schlegel opposes blanket AI bans and special attorney disclosure orders, arguing existing duties already govern responsibility for submitted work. He reports that Louisiana's Supreme Court adopted a reminder-of-existing-duties approach, while leaving open future rule changes. This opposition concerns attorney-facing requirements, distinct from his support for internal staff disclosure to judges. He analogises responsibility for AI-assisted work to signing work prepared by associates or paralegals.
qs: We have enough rules out there to address these two situations.
Louisiana Supreme Court agreed and took the approach and sent a letter to the members of the bar reminding them of all their duties
Today we think the rules that exist cover every issue that we're seeing.
You signed the dotted line, that means you own it.

kp.k: Persistent hallucinations motivate mandatory practical AI education
kp.d: Although resistant to rules for their own sake, Schlegel says continuing hallucination incidents have persuaded him to support one mandatory hour of AI continuing legal education. He wants practical instruction on risks, benefits, tools and settings, not promotional presentations or expert-level technical training. He suggests rapid technological change would provide material for another hour the following year; this is a recommendation, not an adopted requirement.
qs: Thought the hallucinations would stop by now, but now I'm on the bandwagon of we should start mandating one hour CLE
Here are some of the tools, here are some of the settings.
Again, we're not trying to make everybody experts
you're always gonna have good material for another one hour CLE the following year.

kp.k: Effective oversight requires relevant expertise, not merely licensure
kp.d: Schlegel rejects generic human-in-the-loop assurances in favour of the right human: someone with both substantive legal understanding and familiarity with the particular tool. He warns that younger practitioners' technical fluency can exceed their grasp of legal nuance, and that experienced lawyers can become overconfident outside their specialism. His training recommendation is to begin with familiar work in controlled settings, while senior lawyers engage with technology and juniors deliberately learn law.
qs: I hate the terminology human in the loop. It's the right human in the loop.
Because the younger lawyers and judges may not have the scarring necessary to understand the nuance of the law.
just because you're. A labor lawyer doesn't mean you're going to become the best med mal lawyer that ever lived because you'd have a gen AI tool.
So start small, start slow, do something today in a very controlled way so that you can learn the strengths and weaknesses.

kp.k: Human first drafts protect reasoning against confirmation bias
kp.d: Schlegel opposes handing pleadings to AI for a substantive first draft or decision because existing text can steer human reasoning. He recommends designing ambitious systems but restoring deliberate checkpoints before deployment to prevent overdelegation. Judges and staff should struggle with ideas themselves, then use AI to refine expression or finish thoughts. He explicitly exempts routine administrative orders and very simple dispositions from this objection.
qs: I'm talking about confirmation bias.
So that if something is already on a piece of paper, it's gonna be the tail wagging the dog.
you do the first draft, you struggle with the ideas, you struggle with the concepts
use it to clean things up, use it to say something better, use it to finish a thought
I'm not talking about administrative orders.

kp.k: Human adjudication is a social-contract requirement
kp.d: Schlegel makes a normative argument that public adjudication requires accountable human judgment, not algorithmic substitution, even if automation promises speed or consistency. He stresses litigants' voices, the ability to challenge a named judge and the possibility that different models or prompts produce different outcomes. He distinguishes compulsory court proceedings from parties' consensual choice to use AI in mediation or arbitration, which he does not oppose.
qs: we signed up for, we have a dispute, we bring it to the courts, we ask the courts to decide it.
That is an algorithmic decision that was made. And that could change tomorrow because it was asked a different way or the algorithm changed.
That's a decision that was made by parties consensually.
Voice matters and it needs to be handled by a human.

kp.k: AI can assist checking without taking over judicial authorship
kp.d: Schlegel recommends proofreading and citation checking as initial judicial use cases, including looking for spelling errors and misstatements of facts or law. He claims AI can detect issues missed after repeated human rereading. These are practitioner recommendations and assertions of usefulness; the interview provides no accuracy study or measured reliability for these checking tasks.
qs: And it's a great first use case for a judge. Proofread this document for me.
It's not, don't change anything, just proofread this thing for me.
Are there any misstatements of the law? Site check it for me.
It'll catch things that the human eye cannot catch.

kp.k: Advocates should use AI to sharpen briefs and preparation
kp.d: Schlegel recommends critical AI assistance for clearer briefs, analysing opposing arguments and preparing oral argument, conditional on understanding the tools. Suggested methods include simulated questioning by an AI panel and NotebookLM-generated audio discussions of briefs. He distinguishes the advocate's persuasive role from the judge's duty to decide correctly and does not advocate surrendering control over arguments.
qs: Lawyers should be using this to write better arguments to the court.
Again, this always premises you understand how to use it.
Again, you're not turning it over.
Ask these tools to be a panel.
My job is to get it right. Your job is to convince me that you're right.

kp.k: Cloud adoption offers an analogy for AI safeguards
kp.d: Schlegel closes with an optimistic analogy to lawyers' earlier adjustment to cloud storage: initial fear can give way to routine adoption once practitioners understand licensing, confidentiality and settings. For generative AI he recommends avoiding free products, using appropriate settings and preventing training on users' information. This is an analogy and reassurance about professional adaptation, not evidence that any paid service automatically supplies adequate protection.
qs: We learned if you're going to use cloud- based, you need to make sure that you have the right license for the right types of files.
And all of the same lessons are here today for Gen. AI.
Don't use free. Make sure the settings are right. Don't let it to be trained off of you.
That's what lawyers do. We adapt.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Schlegel predicts that integration into trusted enterprise software will increase judicial adoption of generative AI.
pts.d: Schlegel attributes earlier resistance in chambers to unfamiliar products, high token costs and unaffordable implementations. He predicts increased adoption as AI becomes embedded in established legal research and office software. He also describes some courts seeking less constrained tools as their familiarity grows. These are observations and forecasts, not measured adoption results.

pts.k: Schlegel anticipates on-premises AI assisting appellate central staff and clerk's-office intake, subject to funding.
pts.d: He describes a prospective local AI-server project for Louisiana's Fifth Circuit Court of Appeal, intended to support central staff on civil cases and assist intake. This is a planned administrative and staff-support application, not an implemented system with demonstrated savings. Budget approval and competing building-maintenance expenses may prevent or delay deployment.

pts.k: Schlegel says critically used AI can improve appellate briefs and preparation for oral argument.
pts.d: He recommends using AI to clarify lawyers' own writing, challenge opposing briefs, simulate an appellate panel and generate questions for practice. He identifies NotebookLM-generated audio discussions of briefs as another preparation method. His claim is augmentation: a lawyer must understand the tools and critically assess suggestions rather than turn advocacy over to them.

pts.k: Schlegel presents proofreading and citation checking as useful introductory judicial AI applications.
pts.d: He says AI can identify errors missed by a person who has repeatedly read the same document, including spelling mistakes and possible misstatements of fact or law. He recommends requesting checks rather than wholesale rewriting. His description of these uses as safe and useful is practical advice; the interview supplies no accuracy measurements for these tasks and does not establish that AI checking eliminates the need for human verification.

pts.k: Schlegel argues that AI-generated substantive first drafts can anchor judicial reasoning and encourage overdelegation.
pts.d: He describes a risk that an initial AI answer will steer the judge's subsequent reasoning, calling this confirmation bias. He therefore advocates independent engagement with the file and substantive human drafting before AI revision. He distinguishes this from routine administrative orders or very simple dispositions, for which AI drafting may be acceptable. His preferred deployment approach is to design broadly and then insert deliberate controls before implementation.

pts.k: Schlegel says meaningful AI supervision requires relevant legal expertise and tool-specific competence, not merely a licensed human reviewer.
pts.d: He argues that technical fluency does not substitute for legal judgment and that AI does not make a lawyer competent in an unfamiliar specialty. Younger users may lack the experience needed to recognize nuance, while senior lawyers should not simply delegate technology to juniors. He recommends beginning with familiar work, controlled use and progressively more capable tools. He also says different model products behave differently, requiring additional learning when switching.

pts.k: Schlegel says judicial hallucinations pose institutional risks because erroneous AI material can enter orders and precedent.
pts.d: He contrasts sanctions and other consequences for lawyers with the possibility that a judicial error becomes law. He recounts two federal opinions that were recalled and a state-court order containing hallucinated cases supplied by a lawyer. He says judges must scrutinize proposed orders more closely and describes his court's internal policy of approved uses, approved products and staff disclosure to the judge. His support for internal disclosure is distinct from his opposition to blanket attorney disclosure requirements.

pts.k: Schlegel argues that existing professional rules currently address AI misuse, but continuing hallucinations warrant practical mandatory AI education.
pts.d: He opposes blanket generative-AI bans and general requirements that lawyers disclose its use, arguing that signing a filing already entails responsibility for its contents. He reports that Louisiana's Supreme Court reminded lawyers of existing obligations rather than adopting special rules. However, he says persistent hallucination incidents have led him to support a mandatory hour of substantive AI continuing legal education covering risks, benefits, tools and settings. This is a recommendation, not a claim that such a mandate has been adopted.

pts.k: Schlegel rejects AI substitution for judicial decision-making as inconsistent with the social contract, while distinguishing consensual dispute resolution.
pts.d: This is a normative boundary rather than a forecast of technological capability. He argues that litigants are entitled to human judgment and an accountable decision-maker, not outcomes determined by a model that can change with the prompt or algorithm. He distinguishes compulsory court proceedings from parties' consensual choices to use AI in mediation or arbitration.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source relies chiefly on Schlegel's judicial experience, reported incidents, professional judgment and historical analogies rather than systematic AI performance evidence.
pts.d: His adoption and implementation claims draw on experience attempting to introduce tools into his court. His safety claims draw on his drafting guidelines and three judicial hallucination incidents known to him; he gives no case citations and expressly acknowledges uncertainty about the Georgia proceeding and limited examination of it. His expertise argument uses earlier prosecution experiences with PowerPoint and cell-tower records, which are analogies rather than direct evidence about generative AI. His recommendations about advocacy, checking and first drafts are not supported here by experiments, benchmarks or quantified productivity findings. He reports over 200 Judicial AI Consortium sign-ups and over 100 attendees at its initial meeting, indicating interest in peer learning, not demonstrated effectiveness. Earlier accounts of reduced failures to appear concern calendars, reminders and websites, not AI.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Most benefits and risks concern current use at the time of the 2026 interview; expanded adoption and local infrastructure are prospective and conditional.
pts.d: Schlegel gives no dated adoption forecast. Trusted-software integration is already occurring, while the local server project awaits funding. Claimed improvements in advocacy depend on competent, critical use; judicial drafting assistance depends on independent human reasoning and verification. He recommends enterprise tools, appropriate settings and preventing training on users' material. His position that existing rules suffice is explicitly revisable, and continuing hallucinations have already changed his view on mandatory education. His broader optimism about adaptation rests on an analogy with lawyers' earlier adjustment to cloud storage, not a specified transition timetable.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are judges, judicial staff, appellate advocates and litigants; the interview does not predict law-firm market restructuring or employment displacement.
pts.d: Judges gain drafting, checking and administrative assistance but retain responsibility for decisions and oversight. Central staff and clerks are prospective beneficiaries of local AI support, while staff must disclose approved AI use internally. Appellate advocates may improve written persuasion and argument preparation, but remain responsible for filings. Junior practitioners and users working outside their specialties face particular supervision risks. Litigants may be affected by hallucinated orders, model-dependent outcomes and loss of human accountability. Schlegel identifies access to justice and faster processes as topics for consortium exploration, without demonstrating an AI-driven reduction in unmet legal need.
